name: Empress Dowager Cixi
info: Cixi, a Manchu concubine of the Xianfeng Emperor, became empress dowager and regent in 1861 and was the de facto ruler of the Qing Empire for much of the period until her death in 1908.

facts.born: 29 November 1835, probably in Beijing, as Lady Yehe Nara, a Manchu noblewoman of the Yehe Nara clan; daughter of Huizheng of the Bordered Blue Banner
facts.died: 15 November 1908 in the Hall of Graceful Bird at the Middle Sea, Zhongnanhai, Beijing, a day after the Guangxu Emperor; buried in the Eastern Ding Mausoleum
facts.role: Concubine of the Xianfeng Emperor (from 1852; Noble Consort Yi from 1857); Empress Dowager Cixi from 1861; regent for the Tongzhi Emperor from 1861 and for the Guangxu Emperor from 1875; retired from regency 1889, resumed control 1898
facts.known: the Xinyou Coup of 1861 against the eight regents; the Tongzhi Restoration; the suppression of the Hundred Days' Reform in 1898; support for the Boxers and the war on the foreign powers in 1900; the New Policies after her return to Beijing in 1902; the contested reputation she has had since

t: A concubine who could read and write Chinese, Cixi allied with Empress Dowager Ci'an and Prince Gong in 1861 to oust the eight regents appointed by the dying Xianfeng Emperor, and became the only Qing empress dowager to rule as regent.

She backed the Tongzhi Restoration and the learning of Western technology, but stopped the railway and the study abroad programme at times, ended the Guangxu Emperor's Hundred Days' Reform in 1898 and had six reformers beheaded.

Her record is disputed: she has long been portrayed as a ruthless reactionary, while revisionist historians argue she was scapegoated for structural problems, and one of her best-known sources, Backhouse, was later found to have forged much of his material.
dyk: Cixi's physical remains were disturbed in 1928, when the troops of the warlord Sun Dianying dynamited their way into her mausoleum and tore her jewels from her body.
ev: Lady Yehe Nara, the future Cixi, is born
She gives birth to Zaichun, the Xianfeng Emperor's first and only surviving son
After the Xianfeng Emperor's death she and Ci'an oust the eight regents in the Xinyou Coup and begin ruling from behind the curtain
The Tongzhi Emperor dies, and she places her four-year-old nephew on the throne as the Guangxu Emperor
She ends the Hundred Days' Reform and confines the Guangxu Emperor to Ocean Terrace
She supports the Boxers and declares war on the foreign powers; the court flees Beijing for Xi'an
The examination system is abolished among the reforms of the New Policies
She dies a day after the Guangxu Emperor, having chosen his nephew Puyi as successor

sections.early:
Cixi was born on 29 November 1835, the tenth day of the tenth lunar month in the 15th year of the Daoguang Emperor's reign, as Lady Yehe Nara, a Manchu noblewoman of the Yehe Nara clan. Her father, Huizheng, a member of the Bordered Blue Banner, held the title of a third class duke. Palace archives show that he was working in Beijing that year, which indicates that she was born there; the file records her childhood home as Pichai Hutong. She had a sister, Wanzhen, and a brother, Guixiang.

In 1851 she took part in the selection of wives for the Xianfeng Emperor, alongside 60 other candidates, and the emperor's step-mother, Consort Dowager Kangci, chose her as one of the concubines. Another of those chosen was the future Empress Dowager Ci'an. On 26 June 1852 she left her widowed mother's residence and entered the Forbidden City in the sixth rank of consorts, as Noble Lady Lan. She rose to Concubine Yi in 1854 and, on 27 April 1856, gave birth to Zaichun, Xianfeng's first and only surviving son, on which day she became Consort Yi. In 1857 she was raised to Noble Consort Yi, second among the women of the harem after the empress.

Unlike many Manchu women of the household, she could read and write Chinese. Xianfeng had her read palace memorials to him and write instructions on them according to his will, so she became well informed about state affairs.
sections.rise:
In September 1860, in the closing stages of the Second Opium War, the British envoy Harry Parkes and other hostages were arrested, tortured and executed. British and French troops under Lord Elgin attacked Beijing in retaliation and burned the Old Summer Palace. Xianfeng and his entourage, Noble Consort Yi among them, fled to Rehe. The emperor, already showing signs of dementia, fell into depression, turned to alcohol and other drugs, and named eight ministers, headed by Sushun, Zaiyuan and Duanhua, as regents for his heir. He died on 22 August 1861 at Chengde. The heir was his five-year-old son with Noble Consort Yi. Empress Niohuru became Empress Dowager Ci'an, called the East Empress Dowager, and Noble Consort Yi became Empress Dowager Cixi, the West Empress Dowager.

Cixi had no political power from her rank, so she allied herself with Ci'an and with Xianfeng's brothers Prince Gong and Prince Chun, while the regents, led by Sushun, clashed with the empresses dowager. A memorial from Shandong asked that she "listen to politics behind the curtains". She and her son returned to Beijing ahead of the funeral procession, and the regents were dismissed for incompetent negotiations with the foreigners. Of the eight, three were executed: Sushun was beheaded, and Zaiyuan and Duanhua were given white silk to hang themselves with. Cixi declined Prince Gong's suggestion of slow slicing and refused to execute the regents' families. This was the Xinyou Coup, and it made her the only Qing empress dowager to act as regent.
sections.deeds:
In November 1861 Cixi and Ci'an issued edicts that made them the sole decision-makers and changed the boy emperor's reign title from Qixiang to Tongzhi, and Prince Gong was named prince regent. Documents went to the empresses dowager, then to Prince Gong and the Grand Council, and drafts needed their approval. Cixi met every official above provincial governor and had two executed as examples: Qingying, who had tried to bribe his way out of demotion, and He Guiqing, who fled Changzhou before an advancing Taiping army. She put Zeng Guofan, a Han Chinese, in command of the army against the Taipings, which Xiang Army forces defeated in July 1864. The Zongli Yamen, the Tongwen Guan school of 1862 and arsenals and factories date from these years. John K. Fairbank wrote that the Qing survived because of the policy changes known as the Qing Restoration.

She also set limits. Seven British warships bought for the navy arrived under British command and were returned. A railway was forbidden as a danger to the emperors' tombs, and in 1881 she ended the programme of sending children abroad. Tongzhi took personal rule in 1873 and died on 13 January 1875; most historians hold that the cause was smallpox. Cixi had her nephew Zaitian, the four-year-old son of Prince Chun and her sister Wanzhen, made the Guangxu Emperor. Ci'an died in April 1881, probably of a stroke, though rumours that Cixi poisoned her circulated later. Cixi retired from the regency on 5 March 1889, but officials continued to consult her on major decisions.
sections.opponents:
Cixi dismissed Prince Gong in April 1865 on charges that included improper conduct before the empresses dowager. After petitions from the nobility she restored him to the Zongli Yamen but not as prince regent, and he never regained prominence. She quarrelled with the Tongzhi Emperor's wife, Lady Arute, whose grandfather Duanhua had been among the ousted regents. She spied on the couple through eunuchs and ordered them to separate. In August 1874 she and Ci'an appeared at court and made Tongzhi withdraw an edict stripping Prince Gong of his title.

The Guangxu Emperor launched the Hundred Days' Reform in June 1898 under the influence of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao. Cixi, whether fearing for her power or fearing disorder, stepped in. On 21 September 1898 Ronglu took Guangxu to Ocean Terrace, and an edict declared him unfit to be emperor. Six reformers, among them Tan Sitong and Kang's younger brother, were publicly beheaded; Kang fled into exile. In 1894 she had degraded the emperor's favoured Consort Zhen and, by some reports, had her flogged.

Critics charged her with taking the state's revenues as her own. Jasper Becker recalled that visitors to the Summer Palace are told she spent navy funds on its marble boat, leading to the defeat by Japan in 1895. Extensive research by Chinese historians suggests that the navy's decline was caused instead by Guangxu and his adviser Weng Tonghe, who cut naval funding, and the story has been called a false rumour. The anarchist Wu Zhihui wrote of the "vixen empress and vermin emperor".
sections.last:
In 1900 the Boxer Rebellion broke out in northern China. Cixi announced her support for the Boxers and made a formal declaration of war on the Western powers. She said that China had only the people's hearts and minds to depend on, and, on hearing an ultimatum, that she would rather fight to the death than yield. Her forces defeated a small relief force at Langfang but lost the Battle of Beicang, and the Eight-Nation Alliance took Beijing while the court fled to Xi'an. The general Ronglu is reported to have held back artillery and troops from those eager to destroy the legations. Cixi accepted terms that guaranteed no further territory would be given up, and Li Hongzhang signed the Boxer Protocol, with an international force in Beijing and reparations of £67 million.

The court returned to Beijing in January 1902 after about 18 months away. Cixi then sponsored the New Policies, a programme more radical than the one of the reformers she had beheaded. Officials were sent to Japan and Europe, much was modelled on the Meiji reforms, and the examination system ended in 1905. She received the wives of the diplomatic corps.

She died on 15 November 1908 in Zhongnanhai, a day after the Guangxu Emperor, and her chosen heir, his nephew Puyi, succeeded as the Xuantong Emperor. In 2008 tests found the arsenic in Guangxu's remains to be 2,000 times higher than normal. Most historians were inclined to believe Cixi poisoned him, Dai Yi speculated that she feared he would resume his reforms, and others suspect Yuan Shikai; there is no definitive evidence.
sections.legacy:
The widely held view of Cixi is that she was a devious despot who contributed to China's slide into corruption, chaos and revolution, and her conservatism still shapes her image in China. In the People's Republic she was sometimes praised for her role against imperialism in the Boxer Uprising and sometimes reviled as a member of the feudal regime; in 1976 a Palace Museum exhibit of her luxurious goods was used against Jiang Qing.

Early accounts rested on weak sources. China under the Empress Dowager (1910), by J. O. P. Bland and Edmund Backhouse, drew on gossip from palace eunuchs, and Backhouse was later found to have forged much of its source material. The American painter Katharine Carl, who painted her portrait in 1903, described her as kind and considerate and as having an attractive personality.

From the mid-1970s scholars began to revise the picture. Sue Fawn Chung's dissertation was the first study in English to use court documents. Sterling Seagrave portrayed Cixi as caught between a xenophobic Manchu faction and moderates, and Jung Chang's 2013 biography called her the most capable ruler China could have had. Pamela Kyle Crossley replied that Chang's claims had little to do with what is known, and that rewriting Cixi as Catherine the Great or Margaret Thatcher traded historical sense for an illusory icon. Revisionist historians credit her with pragmatic reform, order under imperialist pressure, and support for the Beiyang Army and Peking University.

summary: Cixi (1835–1908), a Manchu concubine, became empress dowager and regent in 1861 after ousting the eight regents and was the de facto ruler of the Qing Empire for much of the time until 1908. She backed technological modernisation, ended the Hundred Days' Reform and declared war on the powers in 1900. Her reputation remains contested.
references: Jung Chang, Empress Dowager Cixi: the concubine who launched modern China (Alfred A. Knopf, 2013)
Sterling Seagrave, Dragon Lady: The Life and Legend of the Last Empress of China (Vintage Books, 1992)
Marina Warner, The Dragon Empress: Life and Times of Tz'u-hsi 1835–1908 (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1972)
notes: Death of the Guangxu Emperor: the lede says Cixi died 'two days after' him, the Death section says 'only a day after'; 'a day after' used.
Tongzhi's death: body gives 13 January 1875, the Issue section gives 12 January 1875; 13 January used. Cause: article says most historians maintain smallpox.
The article's lede says Guangxu was installed on Tongzhi's death 'in 1875' and elsewhere that he 'took over the throne in 1889'; both used as regency and personal rule.

Navy/marble boat: the article says Cixi's blame was 'falsely rumored' and then in the Legacy cites Becker repeating the story as told to visitors; presented as a rumour, attributed to Becker and to Chinese historians as the article does.

Boxer episode: the article credits Ronglu with sabotaging the army and with stopping Dong Fuxiang's troops; stated attributed to the article only in one clause; the article offers no casualty figures for the Boxer war or the Taiping war, so none given. Boxer-related killings of missionaries and Chinese Christians are not described in the article and are left out.

Possible poisoning of Ci'an and Guangxu are given as rumour or inference, as the article does. The article's lede says she 'likely' had Guangxu murdered; the Death section says no definitive evidence; the Death section's version used.

Left out: the alleged deathbed stamps (the article doubts them), the Tongzhi Emperor's brothels and syphilis rumour, the Sun Dianying looting in detail and the bribery rumours (only the one fact in dyk), photographic legacy, honours, the garbled passage about Yu Xunling being 'the son of the French ambassador' (contradicts the article's earlier statement that he was Yu Deling's brother), the Xinhai/1911 aftermath, and popular culture.

Chronology: article says Cixi 'installed her nephew ... at the death of the Tongzhi Emperor in 1875' and 'Guangxu began to take on more responsibilities' in 1886-87; the 'second regency' retirement is 5 March 1889. Retirement is called a 'second regency' there; not used.

The 1894 flogging of Consort Zhen is reported 'according to some reports' in the article; kept hedged. Article text 'the emperor's favoured Consort Zhen' is an inference from 'prefer to spend more time with' her.

The article names the empress dowager's regency a 'return to the helm' in 1875 and calls the 'Hundred Days' Reform' abrupt; in 'opponents' only Cixi's own reasons as the article hedges them are given.
References left empty for the editor.
